kp.k: AI raises a foundational expertise-development problem
kp.d: Roberts proposes that AI-assisted output quality depends on domain expertise multiplied by AI skill. She asks how young people can acquire the expertise and judgment needed to distinguish correct and high-quality outputs if AI performs the foundational work through which expertise was traditionally developed. This is the article's framing argument, not a measured relationship.
qs: In my view, the quality of what you produce with AI depends on a formula: domain expertise x AI skill.
But how can AI-enabled young people learn domain expertise if they rely on AI during their foundational years?
How will they develop the expertise and judgment to know what is right and wrong, and good and bad, in highly fluent and plausible AI outputs?

kp.k: Learning agency distinguishes learning from cognitive offloading
kp.d: Roberts characterises AI's impact as bimodal: the same technology can shortcut understanding or extend learning. Drawing on Bret Taylor's comments about cheating versus curiosity, she proposes learning agency—actively designing one's learning experiences—as the disposition separating these outcomes. The distinction is conceptual rather than an empirically measured distribution.
qs: The impact of AI is bimodal. Same technology, divergent outcomes.
Some people use it to cognitively offload and cheat. Others use it to cognitively extend and learn.
Learning agency is the term I use to describe the disposition to design, engineer, and build your own learning experiences rather than waiting for them to be provided.

kp.k: Production and professional development require simultaneous processes
kp.d: Roberts distinguishes completing an AI-assisted task from developing expertise through that task. She argues that genuine capability develops when users deliberately run both processes within the same workflow, rather than treating a functioning output as sufficient. Her assertion that most users run only the production process is not accompanied by population-level evidence.
qs: The first process is production. Build the thing. Ship the feature. Get the app working.
The second process is development. Build yourself, not just the thing.
Most people run only the first process. The people who develop genuine capability are running both, simultaneously, in the same workflow.
The production process asks: did it work? The development process asks: what did I learn?

kp.k: Software examples illustrate AI-enabled expertise formation
kp.d: Roberts draws on January and February 2026 Lenny's Podcast appearances by Zevi Arnovitz and Lazar Jovanovic. She describes Arnovitz, a Meta product manager without a technical background, and Jovanovic, a forestry engineer working as Lovable's first professional vibe coder, as building revenue-generating software without traditional technical skills. These individual accounts support her proposed mechanism, rather than establishing general outcomes for juniors or lawyers.
qs: A year ago, code was, in his words, "the scariest thing in the world to look at." Today, his engineers at Meta ask him to teach them how to do what he does with AI.
His design judgment, architectural literacy, and debugging instincts developed in months, through AI, not despite it.
Both are building real, revenue-generating software without traditional technical skills.

kp.k: Learners can manufacture practice and targeted coaching
kp.d: The examples show users deliberately constructing learning opportunities: Arnovitz built quizzes, selected colleagues as mentors for particular strengths, and practised segmentation questions for his Meta interview; Jovanovic built an app teaching 18 design styles. Roberts interprets these activities as acquiring coaching rather than merely outsourcing work. Taylor's accounts of his children learning marketing and practising Spanish provide further reported examples.
qs: He mapped each colleague by their specific strength and used each as a targeted mentor: one for product sense, one for methodology, one for systems thinking.
So he used Lovable to build an app that taught him 18 design styles, with prompts to replicate each one.
Both used AI not just to do work but to manufacture practice for themselves.
They weren't outsourcing work; they were insourcing coaching.
This is a tool to amplify agency, not to shortcut understanding a topic.

kp.k: Debriefing and explanations embed learning within production
kp.d: Roberts describes Jovanovic debriefing bugs with AI and recording lessons in a rules file for future application. Arnovitz reflects on successes as well as failures, uses a custom command for explanations, and instructs AI not to flatter him after receiving misleading agreement about different programming concepts. These practices illustrate deliberate feedback generation and attention to understanding while building.
qs: Then he encodes whatever he learns into a rules file, so the AI applies the lesson automatically next time.
Going back and even when you've succeeded, looking and understanding what you did and what you could have done better is critical.
Both are generating feedback that wouldn't otherwise exist.
I am a technical PM in the making. I have mid-level engineering knowledge. I want you to explain what we're currently working on using the 80/20 rule.
The learning happens inside the production workflow, not separate from it.

kp.k: Learning agency extends beyond a growth mindset
kp.d: Roberts distinguishes Dweck's belief that abilities can improve from actively constructing the conditions for improvement. Arnovitz credits reading Mindset with changing his outlook; Roberts also offers her own AI experimentation and development of Dragonfly Thinking as an autobiographical illustration of learning through production. She presents learning agency as applicable across domains, not just coding.
qs: Growth mindset is a belief. Learning agency is an action.
They actively construct the conditions for their own learning.
When I built Dragonfly Thinking, a start-up that uses AI for strategic analysis, the building *was* the learning.
It's what happens when someone takes ownership of their own expertise development — in any domain, through any medium.

kp.k: AI may shift expertise toward architectural understanding
kp.d: Roberts argues that the software examples develop architectural literacy rather than traditional engineering expertise: understanding components, sequence and dependencies while AI handles implementation. She extends this by analogy to junior lawyers learning deal structure through AI contract drafting and medical students developing clinical reasoning through AI exploration. These are conditional possibilities, not demonstrated legal or medical training outcomes: architectural understanding depends on deliberately learning from production.
qs: What they've developed is what I'd call architectural literacy — a conceptual understanding of structure, sequence, composition, and dependencies.
They navigate software at the level of components and relationships, not lines of code.
A junior lawyer who uses AI to draft contracts can develop an understanding of deal structure without having manually drafted every clause.
A medical student who uses AI to explore diagnostic pathways can develop clinical reasoning without having memorised every drug interaction.

And in each case, whether that architectural understanding actually develops depends on whether the person is running the second process: not just producing the output, but learning from the production.

kp.k: Development progresses from building toward judgment
kp.d: Revisiting her earlier 0-to-1 / 1-to-10 / 10-to-100 framework, Roberts proposes learning agency as the missing variable explaining continued development after AI first enables someone to build. Jovanovic's reported progression moves from excitement about building, to speed after one week, to questioning whether the product should be built after two weeks. Roberts emphasises judgment and taste over rapidly changing techniques.
qs: What separates the person who stays at 0-to-1 from the person who keeps developing? I think learning agency is the variable I was missing.
Stage 2, one week later: "Oh, I can build, but I'm not fast enough."
Stage 3, two weeks later: "Wait a minute, should I have even built this in the first place?"
He knows which skills will last (judgment, taste) and which won't (specific techniques): "I'll be wrong on 95% of the things I said today, 3 months from now."

kp.k: Learning agency may itself be developable
kp.d: Roberts cautiously infers from Arnovitz's experience that learning agency might be cultivated rather than innate. She recommends consciously asking what was learned, examining both failures and successes, and encoding lessons. Her concluding prediction is that as AI automates traditional developmental tasks, people who design their own learning will thrive; the article does not establish this through a systematic study.
qs: The potentially hopeful finding from Arnovitz's experience is that learning agency might be something you can develop, not just something that is innate.
If that's right, then the first step is simply seeing the second process clearly enough to start running it.
When something breaks, do you fix it and move on, or do you debrief with the AI on why it broke and encode the lesson?
AI is automating many of the tasks through which expertise was historically built.
In a world where institutions no longer design your learning for you, the people who thrive will be the ones who design it for themselves.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Roberts argues that AI can either shortcut understanding or accelerate expertise development, depending on whether users deliberately learn while producing outputs.
pts.d: This is primarily a cross-domain argument about expertise formation, illustrated through software development. Roberts calls the active construction of one's own learning experiences 'learning agency'. She argues that productive AI use alone does not ensure learning: users must simultaneously build an output and their own understanding. She also argues that AI enables a different kind of expertise, architectural literacy rather than implementation-level knowledge. Her legal example is a junior lawyer developing an understanding of deal structure through AI-assisted contract drafting without manually drafting every clause; this is an illustrative extension, not a reported legal-sector finding. Roberts further suggests that learning agency may itself be developable and predicts that self-directed learners will thrive as AI automates traditional training tasks.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The argument rests on selected practitioner accounts, Roberts's personal experience, and illustrative analogies rather than quantitative evidence or legal-sector research.
pts.d: Roberts draws principally on podcast accounts from Zevi Arnovitz, a nontechnical Meta product manager, and Lazar Jovanovic, a former forestry engineer working as a professional vibe coder at Lovable. She reports that both build revenue-generating software and create practice, explanations, and feedback within their workflows. Their reported behaviours include building quiz apps, requesting explanations, reviewing failures and successes, and encoding lessons into AI instructions. Roberts also uses her experience building Dragonfly Thinking. Bret Taylor's quoted remarks and family anecdotes provide supporting illustrations, while Carol Dweck's growth mindset supplies a conceptual contrast. The source presents no benchmark, controlled comparison, or measured legal learning outcome. Its claims about junior lawyers and medical students are extrapolations from the broader argument.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Roberts describes changes already occurring by April 2026, with individual development over weeks or months, but makes expertise gains conditional on deliberate learning.
pts.d: The article is dated April 2026 and cites practitioner podcasts from January and February 2026. Roberts contrasts Arnovitz's fear of code a year earlier with his current ability to teach engineers about his AI workflows, and describes Jovanovic's development as occurring in months. Jovanovic's quoted stages place shifts in his focus within one and two weeks; these are individual accounts, not general training timelines. The central condition is that users pursue understanding alongside production rather than stop when an output appears successful. The legal analogy is similarly conditional. Roberts's suggestion that learning agency can be developed is explicitly tentative, and her broader prediction about who will thrive has no specified deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are novices, students, and professionals whose foundational work AI can perform, including junior lawyers.
pts.d: Roberts frames the problem as how young people acquire domain expertise and judgment when AI performs foundational tasks. Her software examples concern nontechnical professionals who can now build products while developing conceptual design, architecture, and debugging capabilities. Junior lawyers are presented as potentially learning deal structure through AI-assisted drafting, and medical students as potentially learning clinical reasoning through AI-assisted exploration. Existing domain experts face the complementary task of learning AI skills. The source does not make specific claims about law-firm staffing, legal pricing, client savings, or legal-market competition.
